items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The balance in a main-sequence star between the inward gravitational force and the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation"?
items.answer: stellar equilibrium
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of stellar equilibrium.

items.stem: Explain why fusion of hydrogen in stars is possible at temperatures lower than those predicted classically for overcoming the Coulomb barrier.
items.answer: Quantum tunnelling allows nuclei with less energy than the barrier height to fuse with a small probability; with the enormous number of nuclei in the core, enough reactions occur.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Quantum tunnelling allows nuclei with less energy than the barrier height to fuse with a small probability; with the enormous number of nuclei in the core, enough reactions occur. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Stars shine by burning hydrogen in a chemical reaction with oxygen." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Stars release energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, millions of times more energy per kg than any chemical reaction.
items.markingKey: Stars release energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, millions of times more energy per kg than any chemical reaction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Each completion of the proton–proton chain releases 26.7 MeV. Calculate the number of helium nuclei produced per second in the Sun (luminosity 3.83 × 10²⁶ W) and the rate of hydrogen consumption in kg s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: 26.7 MeV = 4.27 × 10⁻¹² J (A1); N = L/E = 8.97 × 10³⁷ s⁻¹ (M1 A1); 4 protons each: 6.00 × 10¹¹ kg s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A star completes 2.00 × 10³⁸ proton–proton chains per second, each releasing 26.7 MeV. What is its luminosity?
Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Fusion power will solve the world’s energy problems within the next decade."
items.answer: Fusion is promising in the long term, but technical and economic barriers make a decade far too optimistic.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: abundant fuel (deuterium from water, tritium bred from lithium); no long-lived high-level waste or runaway chain reaction; recent milestones such as ignition at NIF in 2022. Arguments against: net energy gain for a whole power plant has not been achieved; materials damaged by 14 MeV neutrons; tritium supply and engineering challenges; ITER first plasma delayed into the 2030s. Supported judgement: Fusion is promising in the long term, but technical and economic barriers make a decade far too optimistic.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stellar equilibrium"?
options: The power received per unit area at the observer, b = L/(4πd²)
The balance in a main-sequence star between the inward gravitational force and the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation
The apparent shift in position of a nearby star against distant background stars as Earth orbits the Sun; distance d (pc) = 1/p (arcsec)
The total power radiated by a star, L = σAT⁴ = 4πR²σT⁴
items.answer: The balance in a main-sequence star between the inward gravitational force and the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation
items.markingKey: B. "stellar equilibrium" is the balance in a main-sequence star between the inward gravitational force and the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation.

items.stem: A tokamak confines plasma using
options: solid steel walls in contact with the plasma
items.answer: strong magnetic fields
items.markingKey: C. Charged particles spiral along field lines.

items.stem: Alessia and a classmate in Accra disagree about nuclear fusion and stellar equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: The brightest stars in the night sky are the most luminous.
Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).
All red stars are small and dim.
The most massive stars live the longest because they have the most hydrogen.
items.answer: Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).

items.stem: Explain the difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
items.answer: Fusion joins light nuclei (left of the BE/A peak) and needs extreme temperatures to overcome repulsion; fission splits heavy nuclei (right of the peak), triggered by neutrons at room temperature; both release energy from increases in binding energy per nucleon.
items.markingKey: Fusion joins light nuclei (left of the BE/A peak) and needs extreme temperatures to overcome repulsion; fission splits heavy nuclei (right of the peak), triggered by neutrons at room temperature; both release energy from increases in binding energy per nucleon. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A star radiates energy at 1.00 × 10²⁶ W. At what rate does it lose mass?
items.markingKey: D. Δm/Δt = L/c² = 1.11 × 10⁹ kg s⁻¹.

items.stem: A student claims: "Gravity and radiation pressure balance because they are equal and opposite forces from fusion." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).
items.markingKey: Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A star completes 5.00 × 10³⁸ proton–proton chains per second, each releasing 26.7 MeV. What is its luminosity?
Explain how a main-sequence star like the Sun maintains stellar equilibrium, and discuss what happens to this equilibrium when hydrogen in the core is exhausted.
items.answer: At every layer the inward gravitational force on the gas is balanced by the outward force due to the pressure gradient of hot gas and radiation, maintained by energy from hydrogen fusion in the core (negative feedback stabilises the rate). When core hydrogen runs out, fusion there stops, pressure falls and the core contracts and heats; hydrogen fusion begins in a shell around the core and the outer layers expand and cool (red giant). Eventually the core becomes hot enough (~10⁸ K) for helium fusion.
items.markingKey: Forces identified (A1); energy source and feedback (R1); core contraction when H exhausted (R1); shell burning and envelope expansion (R1); helium ignition (R1).

items.stem: The Sun’s luminosity is 3.83 × 10²⁶ W and its mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg. (a) Calculate the mass converted to energy each second. (b) The fusion of hydrogen to helium converts 0.7 % of the mass of hydrogen to energy; calculate the mass of hydrogen fused each second. (c) If 10 % of the Sun’s mass is available for core fusion, estimate the Sun’s main-sequence lifetime in years.
The Sun will eventually become
options: a red giant and then a white dwarf
items.answer: a red giant and then a white dwarf
items.markingKey: A. Its mass is below the Chandrasekhar limit.

items.stem: Explain why red giants are more luminous than the Sun although their surface temperature is lower.
items.answer: L = 4πR²σT⁴; a red giant’s radius is tens to hundreds of times the Sun’s, so its surface area is enormous, more than compensating for the lower T⁴.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: L = 4πR²σT⁴; a red giant’s radius is tens to hundreds of times the Sun’s, so its surface area is enormous, more than compensating for the lower T⁴. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the evolution of a low-mass star and the evolution of a high-mass star.
items.answer: Low-mass stars (< ~8 M☉) become red giants, shed planetary nebulae and leave white dwarfs; high-mass stars become red supergiants, fuse up to iron, explode as supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes.
items.markingKey: Low-mass stars (< ~8 M☉) become red giants, shed planetary nebulae and leave white dwarfs; high-mass stars become red supergiants, fuse up to iron, explode as supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Omar writes: "All red stars are small and dim." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Red dwarfs are small and dim, but red giants and supergiants are red (cool) and extremely luminous because they are huge.
items.markingKey: Red dwarfs are small and dim, but red giants and supergiants are red (cool) and extremely luminous because they are huge. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The surface temperature of Proxima Centauri is about 3040 K. Calculate the wavelength at which its emission peaks, and state its colour.
items.answer: 954 nm; red

items.stem: The peak wavelength in the spectrum of a star is 500 nm. What is its surface temperature?
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows that stars evolve along the main sequence from hot to cool."
items.answer: Incorrect: the main sequence is a mass sequence; evolution moves stars off it, not along it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the main sequence is a continuous band from hot luminous to cool dim stars. Arguments against: position on the main sequence is set by mass, not age; stars stay near one point while fusing hydrogen and then move off towards giants; the diagram is a snapshot of many stars, not one star’s track. Supported judgement: Incorrect: the main sequence is a mass sequence; evolution moves stars off it, not along it.

items.stem: Sketch an HR diagram with labelled axes and use it to describe the evolutionary path of (a) a star of 1 M☉ and (b) a star of 15 M☉, from the main sequence to their final states.
items.answer: Axes: luminosity (log, L☉) against temperature (log, decreasing to the right). (a) 1 M☉: main sequence near 5800 K, 1 L☉ for ~10¹⁰ y → moves up and right to red giant branch → helium flash and horizontal branch → asymptotic giant branch → ejects planetary nebula → white dwarf at bottom left, cooling. (b) 15 M☉: upper-left main sequence (~30 000 K, ~10⁴ L☉) for ~10⁷ y → moves right across to red supergiant, fusing successively heavier elements to iron → core collapse supernova → neutron star (or black hole), off the diagram.
items.markingKey: Correct axes with scale direction (A1); 1 M☉ path with stages (R1 R1); 15 M☉ path with stages (R1 R1); final states and reasons (mass limits) (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A plot of stellar luminosity against surface temperature (decreasing to the right), on which stars fall into groups such as the main sequence, giants, supergiants and white dwarfs"?
items.answer: Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram.

items.stem: Define the term "main sequence".
items.answer: The band on the HR diagram from hot luminous stars to cool dim stars, occupied by stars fusing hydrogen in their cores
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the band on the HR diagram from hot luminous stars to cool dim stars, occupied by stars fusing hydrogen in their cores. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and stellar evolution is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Tariq.)
options: D = 1/p: twice the parallax means half the distance.
Stars release energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, millions of times more energy per kg than any chemical reaction.
The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.
The HR diagram shows how a single star moves along the main sequence as it ages.
items.answer: The HR diagram shows how a single star moves along the main sequence as it ages.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Stars stay at almost the same place on the main sequence while fusing core hydrogen; they leave it (towards giants) when core hydrogen runs out.

items.stem: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but star P is 100 times more luminous than star Q. The ratio of their radii R_P/R_Q is
items.markingKey: D. L ∝ R² at fixed T.

items.stem: Sirius A has a surface temperature of 9500 K and a luminosity of 25 L☉. State its region on the HR diagram and explain what this tells you about its size and stage of evolution.
items.answer: main-sequence star; radius ≈ 2.6 R☉
items.markingKey: Region: main-sequence star (A1); size inferred from L = 4πR²σT⁴ (R1); evolutionary stage consistent with region (R1).

items.stem: Arcturus has a surface temperature of 4290 K. At what wavelength does its emission peak?
items.answer: 676 nm
items.markingKey: A. λ = b/T = 676 nm.

items.stem: Barnard’s Star has a surface temperature of 3130 K. At what wavelength does its emission peak?
items.answer: 927 nm
items.markingKey: D. λ = b/T = 927 nm.

items.stem: The peak wavelength in the spectrum of a star is 300 nm. What is its surface temperature?
Aldebaran has radius 20.0 R☉ and temperature 3900 K; Betelgeuse has radius 168 R☉ and temperature 3500 K. Calculate the ratio of their luminosities L(Aldebaran)/L(Betelgeuse).

Star X has surface temperature 3500 K and luminosity 4.0 × 10⁴ L☉; star Y has surface temperature 14 000 K and luminosity 0.010 L☉. (a) Calculate the ratio of their radii R_X/R_Y. (b) Identify each type of star and its position on the HR diagram. (c) Describe the evolutionary connection between the two types.
items.answer: (a) R ∝ √L/T²: R_X/R_Y = √(4.0 × 10⁶) × (14 000/3500)² = 2000 × 16 = 3.2 × 10⁴; (b) X: red supergiant (top right); Y: white dwarf (bottom left); (c) not directly: a red supergiant is too massive and will end as a neutron star or black hole; white dwarfs come from low-mass stars after the red-giant and planetary-nebula stages.
items.markingKey: (a) R ∝ √L/T²: R_X/R_Y = √(4.0 × 10⁶) × (14 000/3500)² = 2000 × 16 = 3.2 × 10⁴; (b) X: red supergiant (top right); Y: white dwarf (bottom left); (c) not directly: a red supergiant is too massive and will end as a neutron star or black hole; white dwarfs come from low-mass stars after the red-giant and planetary-nebula stages.

items.stem: "The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows that stars evolve along the main sequence from hot to cool." Discuss.
items.answer: Incorrect: the main sequence is a mass sequence; evolution moves stars off it, not along it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the main sequence is a continuous band from hot luminous to cool dim stars. Arguments against: position on the main sequence is set by mass, not age; stars stay near one point while fusing hydrogen and then move off towards giants; the diagram is a snapshot of many stars, not one star’s track. Supported judgement: Incorrect: the main sequence is a mass sequence; evolution moves stars off it, not along it. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "luminosity"?
options: The time a star spends fusing hydrogen in its core, approximately proportional to M/L and hence to M^(−2.5)
The balance in a main-sequence star between the inward gravitational force and the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation
The total power radiated by a star, L = σAT⁴ = 4πR²σT⁴
A small, hot, dense remnant of a low-mass star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure, no longer fusing
items.answer: The total power radiated by a star, L = σAT⁴ = 4πR²σT⁴
items.markingKey: C. "luminosity" is the total power radiated by a star, L = σAT⁴ = 4πR²σT⁴.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "The brightest stars in the night sky are the most luminous." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance; many bright stars (e.g. Sirius) appear bright mainly because they are close.
items.markingKey: Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance; many bright stars (e.g. Sirius) appear bright mainly because they are close. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a parsec and a light-year.
items.answer: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year (9.46 × 10¹⁵ m); a parsec is defined by a parallax of one arcsecond (3.09 × 10¹⁶ m = 3.26 ly).
items.markingKey: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year (9.46 × 10¹⁵ m); a parsec is defined by a parallax of one arcsecond (3.09 × 10¹⁶ m = 3.26 ly). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A star of luminosity 9.58 × 10²⁷ W is 2 pc from Earth. What is its apparent brightness?
items.markingKey: B. b = L/(4πd²) with d = 6.18 × 10¹⁶ m: 2.00 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

items.stem:
A student tests the Stefan–Boltzmann law using a filament lamp of surface area 3.00 × 10⁻⁵ m²; the filament temperature T is estimated from its resistance and the power P supplied is measured. Theory: P = eσAT⁴, where e is the emissivity.

T / K | P / W
1200 | 1.26
1400 | 2.24
1600 | 3.84
1800 | 6.24
2000 | 9.66
2200 | 13.56

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the emissivity e of the filament. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the emissivity with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) P (y) against T⁴ (x); (b) gradient ≈ 5.83 × 10⁻¹³ W K⁻⁴; (c) 0.343; (d) 0.343 ± 0.01
items.markingKey: (a) P (y) against T⁴ (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 5.83 × 10⁻¹³ W K⁻⁴ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) e = gradient/(σA) = 0.343 (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 0.01 ; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: The star Vega has a parallax of 0.130 arcsec, an apparent brightness of 2.2 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² and a peak emission wavelength of 302 nm. (a) Determine its distance. (b) Determine its luminosity. (c) Determine its surface temperature and radius. (d) State its likely position on the HR diagram.
items.answer: (a) d = 7.69 pc = 2.38 × 10¹⁷ m; (b) L = 4πd²b = 1.6 × 10²⁸ W (≈ 41 L☉); (c) T = 2.90 × 10⁻³/302 × 10⁻⁹ = 9600 K; R = √(L/4πσT⁴) = 1.6 × 10⁹ m (≈ 2.3 R☉); (d) upper main sequence (A-type star).
items.markingKey: d = 1/p converted to m (A1); L (M1 A1); T by Wien (A1); R from Stefan–Boltzmann (A1); main sequence (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The distance at which a star has a parallax angle of one arcsecond, 1 pc = 3.26 ly = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m"?
items.answer: parsec
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of parsec.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about stellar luminosity, apparent brightness and parallax distances is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Amara.)
options: Stars release energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, millions of times more energy per kg than any chemical reaction.
The brightest stars in the night sky are the most luminous.
Stars stay at almost the same place on the main sequence while fusing core hydrogen; they leave it (towards giants) when core hydrogen runs out.
Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).
items.answer: The brightest stars in the night sky are the most luminous.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance; many bright stars (e.g. Sirius) appear bright mainly because they are close.

items.stem: Why are parallax measurements made six months apart?
options: Earth is then at opposite ends of its orbit, giving the largest baseline (2 AU)
the Sun is closest to the star
the star moves in six months
items.answer: Earth is then at opposite ends of its orbit, giving the largest baseline (2 AU)
items.markingKey: A. Maximum baseline.

items.stem: Explain why two stars with the same apparent brightness need not have the same luminosity.
items.answer: b = L/(4πd²); a more luminous star further away can appear as bright as a less luminous star nearby, so distance must also be known.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: b = L/(4πd²); a more luminous star further away can appear as bright as a less luminous star nearby, so distance must also be known. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Arcturus has a luminosity of 6.51 × 10²⁸ W and is 11.3 pc away. Calculate its apparent brightness at Earth.
A star has a parallax angle of 0.1 arcsec. What is its distance?
items.markingKey: B. d (pc) = 1/p (arcsec) = 10.0 pc; ×3.26 would give light-years.

items.stem: Two stars appear equally bright from Earth. Star X is 10 times further away than star Y. Determine the ratio of their luminosities L_X/L_Y, and if both have the same temperature, the ratio of their radii.
items.answer: L ratio 100; radius ratio 10
items.markingKey: b = L/(4πd²) equal → L ∝ d² (M1): 10² = 100 (A1); same T → L ∝ R² → R ratio 10 (A1).

items.stem: "Parallax is the foundation of all astronomical distance measurements." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is the essential first rung of the distance ladder, though other methods are needed beyond our galaxy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is a direct geometric method with no assumptions about stars; it calibrates Cepheid variables and other standard candles (the distance ladder). Arguments against: it only reaches nearby stars; galaxy distances need standard candles and redshift; errors propagate up the ladder. Supported judgement: It is the essential first rung of the distance ladder, though other methods are needed beyond our galaxy. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

T / K | P / W

(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the emissivity with its absolute uncertainty. [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "For main-sequence stars, luminosity is approximately proportional to mass to the power 3.5, L ∝ M^3.5"?
items.answer: mass–luminosity relation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of mass–luminosity relation.

items.stem: A star cluster contains only main-sequence stars below 2 M☉ plus many red giants. This suggests that
options: the cluster is old enough for stars above ~2 M☉ to have left the main sequence
items.answer: the cluster is old enough for stars above ~2 M☉ to have left the main sequence
items.markingKey: A. Turn-off mass indicates age.

items.stem: Using L ∝ M^3.5, what is the luminosity of a 15 M☉ main-sequence star in solar units?
"The most massive stars live the longest because they have the most hydrogen." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Massive stars burn their fuel so fast (L ∝ M^3.5) that they live much shorter lives (∝ M^−2.5).
items.markingKey: Massive stars burn their fuel so fast (L ∝ M^3.5) that they live much shorter lives (∝ M^−2.5). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Supernovae are essential for the existence of life on Earth."
items.answer: Supernovae are a major source of the heavy elements and dispersal needed for rocky planets and life, though not the only source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they disperse elements made in stars (C, O, Fe) into space; r-process elements formed in explosive events; shock waves may trigger star formation (possibly the Solar System). Arguments against: many heavy elements also come from neutron-star mergers and AGB stars; nearby supernovae can be harmful to life. Supported judgement: Supernovae are a major source of the heavy elements and dispersal needed for rocky planets and life, though not the only source.

items.stem: More massive main-sequence stars have
items.answer: shorter lifetimes
items.markingKey: A. Lifetime ∝ M^−2.5.

items.stem: A teacher in Toronto asks a class to choose the one correct statement about main sequence lifetime and stellar remnants. Which statement should be chosen?
options: The most massive stars live the longest because they have the most hydrogen.
The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.
All red stars are small and dim.
The HR diagram shows how a single star moves along the main sequence as it ages.
items.answer: The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a neutron star and a white dwarf.
items.answer: A white dwarf (≤ 1.4 M☉, Earth-sized) is supported by electron degeneracy pressure; a neutron star (1.4–3 M☉, ~10 km radius) is supported by neutron degeneracy pressure and is far denser.
items.markingKey: A white dwarf (≤ 1.4 M☉, Earth-sized) is supported by electron degeneracy pressure; a neutron star (1.4–3 M☉, ~10 km radius) is supported by neutron degeneracy pressure and is far denser. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A main-sequence star has luminosity 1000 L☉. Estimate its mass and the likely type of its final remnant.
items.answer: 7.20 M☉; white dwarf
items.markingKey: M = L^(1/3.5) (M1) = 7.20 M☉ (A1); low/intermediate mass → white dwarf (R1).

items.stem: The Sun’s main-sequence lifetime is 10¹⁰ years. What is the approximate lifetime of a 2 M☉ star? (L ∝ M^3.5)
items.answer: 1.77 × 10⁹ years

items.stem: A star of 20 M☉ and a star of 0.5 M☉ form together in the same cloud. (a) Use L ∝ M^3.5 to compare their luminosities. (b) Compare their main-sequence lifetimes, given the Sun’s is 10¹⁰ years. (c) Describe and explain the different end states of the two stars. (d) Discuss whether either star could host a planet with life that evolved as on Earth.
items.answer: (a) L ratio = 40^3.5 ≈ 4 × 10⁵ (20 M☉: ~3.6 × 10⁴ L☉; 0.5 M☉: ~0.09 L☉); (b) 20 M☉: 10¹⁰ × 20^−2.5 ≈ 5.6 × 10⁶ y; 0.5 M☉: ≈ 5.7 × 10¹⁰ y; (c) the massive star becomes a red supergiant, explodes as a core-collapse supernova and leaves a neutron star or black hole; the low-mass star will eventually become a white dwarf (after ~10¹⁰+ years); (d) the 20 M☉ star lives far too briefly for complex life (Earth took ~4 × 10⁹ y); the 0.5 M☉ star lives long enough but its habitable zone is close in, with flares and tidal locking as complications.
items.markingKey: Luminosity ratio (A1); lifetimes (M1 A1); end states with mass limits (R1); evaluation of habitability using timescales (R1 R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "main sequence"?
options: The maximum mass (about 1.4 M☉) of a white dwarf that can be supported by electron degeneracy pressure
The band on the HR diagram from hot luminous stars to cool dim stars, occupied by stars fusing hydrogen in their cores
An extremely dense stellar remnant of about 1.4–3 M☉ supported by neutron degeneracy pressure, formed in a core-collapse supernova
The balance in a main-sequence star between the inward gravitational force and the outward pressure of hot gas and radiation
items.answer: The band on the HR diagram from hot luminous stars to cool dim stars, occupied by stars fusing hydrogen in their cores
items.markingKey: B. "main sequence" is the band on the HR diagram from hot luminous stars to cool dim stars, occupied by stars fusing hydrogen in their cores.

items.stem: Fusion in the core of the Sun occurs at a temperature of about
items.markingKey: B. Core temperature ~15 million K.

items.stem: Define the term "stellar parallax".
items.answer: The apparent shift in position of a nearby star against distant background stars as Earth orbits the Sun; distance d (pc) = 1/p (arcsec)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the apparent shift in position of a nearby star against distant background stars as Earth orbits the Sun; distance d (pc) = 1/p (arcsec). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a remnant core above about 3 M☉ becomes a black hole.
items.answer: Above the Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit not even neutron degeneracy pressure can resist gravity, so the core collapses until its escape speed exceeds c and an event horizon forms.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Above the Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit not even neutron degeneracy pressure can resist gravity, so the core collapses until its escape speed exceeds c and an event horizon forms. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "All red stars are small and dim." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Red dwarfs are small and dim, but red giants and supergiants are red (cool) and extremely luminous because they are huge.
items.markingKey: Red dwarfs are small and dim, but red giants and supergiants are red (cool) and extremely luminous because they are huge. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
items.answer: Fusion joins light nuclei (left of the BE/A peak) and needs extreme temperatures to overcome repulsion; fission splits heavy nuclei (right of the peak), triggered by neutrons at room temperature; both release energy from increases in binding energy per nucleon.
items.markingKey: Fusion joins light nuclei (left of the BE/A peak) and needs extreme temperatures to overcome repulsion; fission splits heavy nuclei (right of the peak), triggered by neutrons at room temperature; both release energy from increases in binding energy per nucleon. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how the luminosity, temperature and radius of a star are linked.
items.answer: A star approximates a black body, so its luminosity equals σT⁴ multiplied by its surface area 4πR²; knowing any two quantities gives the third.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A star approximates a black body, so its luminosity equals σT⁴ multiplied by its surface area 4πR²; knowing any two quantities gives the third. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a white dwarf and a neutron star.
items.answer: A white dwarf (≤ 1.4 M☉, Earth-sized) is supported by electron degeneracy pressure; a neutron star (1.4–3 M☉, ~10 km radius) is supported by neutron degeneracy pressure and is far denser.
items.markingKey: A white dwarf (≤ 1.4 M☉, Earth-sized) is supported by electron degeneracy pressure; a neutron star (1.4–3 M☉, ~10 km radius) is supported by neutron degeneracy pressure and is far denser. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A star with three times the Sun’s mass leaves the main sequence. It will next become
items.answer: a red giant
items.markingKey: A. Shell burning makes the envelope expand.

items.stem: A star has a luminosity of 3.83 × 10²⁶ W. Calculate the rate at which it loses mass by converting mass into radiated energy.
A star has a parallax angle of 0.2 arcsec. What is its distance?
items.markingKey: A. d (pc) = 1/p (arcsec) = 5.00 pc; ×3.26 would give light-years.

items.stem: A student claims: "The most massive stars live the longest because they have the most hydrogen." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Massive stars burn their fuel so fast (L ∝ M^3.5) that they live much shorter lives (∝ M^−2.5).
items.markingKey: Massive stars burn their fuel so fast (L ∝ M^3.5) that they live much shorter lives (∝ M^−2.5). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The peak wavelength in the spectrum of a star is 250 nm. What is its surface temperature?
A star completes 1.00 × 10³⁸ proton–proton chains per second, each releasing 26.7 MeV. What is its luminosity?
Star P has 3 times the radius and 3 times the surface temperature of star Q. What is L_P/L_Q?
items.markingKey: C. L ∝ R²T⁴ = 3² × 3⁴ = 729.

items.stem: A main-sequence star has luminosity 10000 L☉. Estimate its mass and the likely type of its final remnant.
items.answer: 13.9 M☉; neutron star or black hole
items.markingKey: M = L^(1/3.5) (M1) = 13.9 M☉ (A1); massive → supernova → neutron star/black hole (R1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The HR diagram is the most important single tool in stellar astrophysics."
items.answer: It is a central organising tool that, combined with physical models, underpins our understanding of stellar evolution.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows stellar groups and evolution; allows distances by spectroscopic parallax; cluster HR diagrams give ages (turn-off point). Arguments against: it summarises but does not explain; models of nuclear fusion and stellar structure are needed; requires accurate distances and luminosities. Supported judgement: It is a central organising tool that, combined with physical models, underpins our understanding of stellar evolution.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Fusion power will solve the world’s energy problems within the next decade."
items.answer: Fusion is promising in the long term, but technical and economic barriers make a decade far too optimistic.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: abundant fuel (deuterium from water, tritium bred from lithium); no long-lived high-level waste or runaway chain reaction; recent milestones such as ignition at NIF in 2022. Arguments against: net energy gain for a whole power plant has not been achieved; materials damaged by 14 MeV neutrons; tritium supply and engineering challenges; ITER first plasma delayed into the 2030s. Supported judgement: Fusion is promising in the long term, but technical and economic barriers make a decade far too optimistic. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Parallax is the foundation of all astronomical distance measurements." Discuss.
items.answer: It is the essential first rung of the distance ladder, though other methods are needed beyond our galaxy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is a direct geometric method with no assumptions about stars; it calibrates Cepheid variables and other standard candles (the distance ladder). Arguments against: it only reaches nearby stars; galaxy distances need standard candles and redshift; errors propagate up the ladder. Supported judgement: It is the essential first rung of the distance ladder, though other methods are needed beyond our galaxy. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A main-sequence star has 6 times the mass of the Sun. (a) Using L ∝ M^3.5, estimate its luminosity. (b) Estimate its main-sequence lifetime given the Sun’s is 1.0 × 10¹⁰ years. (c) Describe its likely evolution and final state, referring to the Chandrasekhar limit.
items.answer: (a) 6^3.5 ≈ 530 L☉; (b) 10¹⁰ × 6^−2.5 ≈ 1.1 × 10⁸ years; (c) it becomes a red giant, fuses helium (and possibly carbon), sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula; its core, below 1.4 M☉, becomes a carbon–oxygen white dwarf.
items.markingKey: (a) 6^3.5 ≈ 530 L☉; (b) 10¹⁰ × 6^−2.5 ≈ 1.1 × 10⁸ years; (c) it becomes a red giant, fuses helium (and possibly carbon), sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula; its core, below 1.4 M☉, becomes a carbon–oxygen white dwarf.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A small, hot, dense remnant of a low-mass star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure, no longer fusing"?
items.answer: white dwarf
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of white dwarf.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "plasma".
items.answer: A state of matter of separated nuclei and electrons at very high temperatures, as in stellar cores and fusion reactors
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a state of matter of separated nuclei and electrons at very high temperatures, as in stellar cores and fusion reactors. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: If the distance to a star doubles, its apparent brightness
items.answer: falls to one quarter
items.markingKey: B. b ∝ 1/d².

items.stem: Ana is revising main sequence lifetime and stellar remnants. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Stars shine by burning hydrogen in a chemical reaction with oxygen.
The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.
All red stars are small and dim.
Gravity and radiation pressure balance because they are equal and opposite forces from fusion.
items.answer: The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. The Sun’s core remnant will be well below 1.4 M☉, so it will become a white dwarf.

items.stem: Rigel has a surface temperature of 12100 K and a luminosity of 1.2 × 10⁵ L☉. State its region on the HR diagram and explain what this tells you about its size and stage of evolution.
items.answer: supergiant; radius ≈ 260 R☉
items.markingKey: Region: supergiant (A1); size inferred from L = 4πR²σT⁴ (R1); evolutionary stage consistent with region (R1).

items.stem: Mateo and a classmate in Lisbon disagree about nuclear fusion and stellar equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: The HR diagram shows how a single star moves along the main sequence as it ages.
Stars shine by burning hydrogen in a chemical reaction with oxygen.
The brightest stars in the night sky are the most luminous.
Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).
items.answer: Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Gravity pulls inward from the star’s mass; the outward pressure gradient comes from hot gas and radiation heated by fusion; they balance at each layer (hydrostatic equilibrium).

items.stem: Star A has twice the radius and the same temperature as star B. The luminosity of A is
items.answer: 4 times that of B
items.markingKey: A. L ∝ R².

items.stem: Explain why elements heavier than iron are not produced by fusion in stellar cores.
items.answer: Fusing nuclei beyond iron decreases binding energy per nucleon and absorbs energy; heavier elements are made by neutron capture (s- and r-processes) in giant stars, supernovae and neutron-star mergers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fusing nuclei beyond iron decreases binding energy per nucleon and absorbs energy; heavier elements are made by neutron capture (s- and r-processes) in giant stars, supernovae and neutron-star mergers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a white dwarf and a red giant.
items.answer: A red giant is a large, cool, luminous star still undergoing fusion in a shell; a white dwarf is a small, hot, dim stellar remnant that is no longer fusing and slowly cools.
items.markingKey: A red giant is a large, cool, luminous star still undergoing fusion in a shell; a white dwarf is a small, hot, dim stellar remnant that is no longer fusing and slowly cools. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A star radiates energy at 4.00 × 10²⁶ W. At what rate does it lose mass?
items.markingKey: D. Δm/Δt = L/c² = 4.44 × 10⁹ kg s⁻¹.

items.stem: Omar writes: "A star with twice the parallax angle is twice as far away." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: d = 1/p: twice the parallax means half the distance.
items.markingKey: d = 1/p: twice the parallax means half the distance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The Sun’s main-sequence lifetime is 10¹⁰ years. What is the approximate lifetime of a 4 M☉ star? (L ∝ M^3.5)
items.answer: 3.12 × 10⁸ years

items.stem: Barnard’s Star has a luminosity of 0.00350 L☉ (L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W) and a surface temperature of 3130 K. Calculate its radius and deduce its type.
items.answer: 1.40 × 10⁸ m (0.201 R☉); main-sequence star
items.markingKey: L = 4πR²σT⁴ (M1); R = √(L/(4πσT⁴)) = 1.40 × 10⁸ m (A1); ≈ 0.201 R☉ → main-sequence star (R1).

items.stem: Two protons approach head-on, each with the mean kinetic energy (3/2)k_BT at T = 1.50 × 10⁷ K (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹). Estimate their distance of closest approach and comment on whether fusion is possible classically.
items.answer: 3.71 × 10⁻¹³ m; far larger than ~10⁻¹⁵ m, so fusion requires tunnelling (or higher energies)
items.markingKey: Eₖ each = 3.10 × 10⁻¹⁶ J (A1); 2Eₖ = ke²/d (M1); d = 3.71 × 10⁻¹³ m (A1); compare with range of strong force (R1).

items.stem: A star 10 pc away has an apparent brightness of 1.20 × 10⁻¹¹ W m⁻². Determine its luminosity in watts and in solar luminosities.
Given L ∝ M^3.5 and a solar lifetime of 1.0 × 10¹⁰ y, what is the main-sequence lifetime of a 3 M☉ star?
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows that stars evolve along the main sequence from hot to cool."
items.answer: Incorrect: the main sequence is a mass sequence; evolution moves stars off it, not along it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the main sequence is a continuous band from hot luminous to cool dim stars. Arguments against: position on the main sequence is set by mass, not age; stars stay near one point while fusing hydrogen and then move off towards giants; the diagram is a snapshot of many stars, not one star’s track. Supported judgement: Incorrect: the main sequence is a mass sequence; evolution moves stars off it, not along it.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Sun will run out of fuel in the near future."
items.answer: No: although the consumption rate is huge, the Sun has billions of years of core hydrogen remaining.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fusion consumes about 6 × 10¹¹ kg of hydrogen per second. Arguments against: the Sun contains ~10³⁰ kg of hydrogen; only the core fuses; the main-sequence lifetime is ~10¹⁰ years, with about 5 × 10⁹ years remaining. Supported judgement: No: although the consumption rate is huge, the Sun has billions of years of core hydrogen remaining. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:
A student tests the Stefan–Boltzmann law using a filament lamp of surface area 3.00 × 10⁻⁵ m²; the filament temperature T is estimated from its resistance and the power P supplied is measured. Theory: P = eσAT⁴, where e is the emissivity.

T / K | P / W
1200 | 1.38
1400 | 2.62
1600 | 4.39
1800 | 7.06
2000 | 11.16
2200 | 16.10

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the emissivity e of the filament. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State the emissivity with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) P (y) against T⁴ (x); (b) gradient ≈ 6.93 × 10⁻¹³ W K⁻⁴; (c) 0.407; (d) 0.407 ± 0.02
items.markingKey: (a) P (y) against T⁴ (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 6.93 × 10⁻¹³ W K⁻⁴ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) e = gradient/(σA) = 0.407 (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 0.02 ; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: "Supernovae are essential for the existence of life on Earth." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Supernovae are a major source of the heavy elements and dispersal needed for rocky planets and life, though not the only source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they disperse elements made in stars (C, O, Fe) into space; r-process elements formed in explosive events; shock waves may trigger star formation (possibly the Solar System). Arguments against: many heavy elements also come from neutron-star mergers and AGB stars; nearby supernovae can be harmful to life. Supported judgement: Supernovae are a major source of the heavy elements and dispersal needed for rocky planets and life, though not the only source. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
